newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Daimler puts bet on alternative power engine.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Daimler puts bet on alternative power engine.

text.p: Daimler-Benz AG has placed a bet on its vision of the alternative-powered vehicle for the future, saying on Monday it bought a 25 percent stake in a Canadian firm that has developed a hydrogen fuel engine.

Daimler, which builds Mercedes vehicles, said it bought the stake in Ballard Power Systems Inc of Vancouver as part of plans for the two to develop the engine, which relies on so-called "fuel cell technology", for passenger vehicles.

The fuel cell engine, which is expected to be used in Chicago city buses by 1998, combines hydrogen gas derived from natural gas, methanol or hydrogen with oxygen to produce an electric current which can then be used to power a vehicle.

Fuel cells, along with hybrid engines, have overtaken the battery as the most likely power plant for future zero-emission cars since batteries are seen as being too expensive and having limited performance, according to industry officials.

But alternative fuel engines are not expected to replace conventional engines anytime soon. A recent report by the London-based Economist Intelligence Unit predicted conventional engines will provide 90 percent of power for the next 15 years.

Ballard and Daimler began joint efforts in 1993 to develop Ballard's proprietary zero-emission engine. Daimler said the new deal calls for the two companies to invest about 400 million marks to develop the engine for serial production.

"Daimler-Benz has set itself the objective of being in a position to supply fuel-cell powered vehicles in just a few years time at a purchase price not considerably different from those of cars with internal combustion engines," Daimler said.
The research, aimed at reducing the size and cost of the new engine, will be done through a joint venture in which Daimler will hold a two-third stake and Ballard one-third.
"We need to lower the cost and weight and also the volume by one-sixth from the current size for it to be competitive with an ordinary engine," a Daimler spokesman told Reuters.
Another company will be responsible for for global sales of the engine. It will be formed by the joint venture and Ballard each taking a 50 percent stake, Daimler said.

Juergen Hubbert, the Daimler management board member responsible for Mercedes passenger cars, said the fuel cell engine currently has "the greatest opportunity of presenting a serious challenge to the internal combustion engine".
"We intend to be the first to supply the market with a serious production vehicle incorporating fuel cell drive," Hubbert said.

One Daimler official said the engine would likely be targeted for Mercedes' new A-class compact vehicle and designed to meet looming regulatory requirements in the United States, particularly in California, for vehicles with reduced or no emissions.
"It will be some years after the year 2000 when you see the engine in vehicles, likely from 2005 to 2010," the official said, noting a new research car was under development.

Fuel cell engines have come into vogue as battery technology, which has been around for almost as long as the internal engine, has failed to make the leap from slow, limited-range use into a regular car.
When pure hydrogen is used, a fuel cell engine only produces water vapour. And the use of methanol reduces the amount of carbon dioxide to about half of current internal combustion engines.
Daimler in 1994 created the original research vehicle for the fuel cell engine, which was dubbed NECAR I. It was followed in 1996 by a vehicle with a considerably smaller engine.
